author: Bryan Rolli
title: 8 Way Underrated Tech-Thrash Bands - NewsBreak
text:
By Bryan Rolli ,
12 hours ago
Here are eight severely underrated technical thrash metal bands that every headbanger needs to know.
Now, listen: Technical thrash was not exactly a widespread musical phenomenon that spawned tons of chart-topping bands. Even within the confines of thrash, it maintained a cult popularity and many of its best bands had fairly brief careers.
So really, when we say underrated technical thrash metal bands , we’re basically just saying good technical thrash metal bands with the exception of Voivod and Annihilator , who both enjoyed modest commercial success and have sustained decades-long careers, as well as a couple of Megadeth ‘s most musically advanced eras.
READ MORE: The 5 Best Technical Thrash Albums (Ranked)
Why These Great Technical Thrash Bands Struggled to Break Out The technical thrash bands on this list failed to thrive commercially for a variety of reasons. Some of them were doomed by location: As thrash exploded on both U.S. coasts, these bands struggled to find their footing in Europe or, even worse, the Midwest.
Others had promising starts but failed to maintain their momentum, subsequently getting dropped from their labels or disbanding due to frustration and a lack of resources.
And frankly, some of these bands just went over people’s heads.
Although technical thrash didn’t spawn a slew of successful bands, it had a major influence on other subgenres — notably technical death metal. Death leader Chuck Schuldiner cited Watchtower, arguably the true progenitors of technical thrash, as a big influence on his own band — and if it’s good enough for Chuck, it’s good enough for you, dammit.
We hope you see some bands you already know and love while also finding some new gems on the following list of eight severely underrated technical thrash metal bands.
8 Severely Underrated Technical Thrash Metal Bands Some were plagued by isolation and poor distribution. Others simply went over listeners' heads. Gallery Credit: Bryan Rolli Kenn Nardi, YouTube Anacrusis As thrash metal was taking both coasts by storm in the mid-‘80s, Anacrusis were stuck in the relative no man’s land of St. Louis. So they had little way of getting their speedy, sophisticated technical thrash sound to the masses.
Then again, maybe headbangers just weren’t ready for Anacrusis’ progressive, panoramic take on the genre.
The band defied all preconceived notions of thrash on 1991’s Manic Impressions and 1993’s Screams and Whispers , going deep into progressive territory while still packing a one-two punch of savage riffs and pulverizing grooves. Anacrusis were doomed to obscurity, but real heads know they were one of the most interesting thrash bands of their time. Metal Blade Records, YouTube Artillery As thrash was taking the U.S. coasts by storm in the early ‘80s, Artillery were busy bringing the sound to the good headbangers of Denmark, beginning with 1985’s Fear of Tomorrow .
The band’s fiery twin-guitar attack and sophisticated song structures would have made them standouts in the tech-thrash scene already. But Artillery’s secret weapon was vocalist Flemming Ronsdorf, whose sandpapery, falsetto scream sounded like a cross between Overkill's Bobby Blitz and Accept's Udo Dirkschneider.
Artillery reached the peak of their powers on 1990’s By Inheritance . They broke up the following year but have since reformed and released a steady stream of albums through 2021’s X . Батя Махно, YouTube Coroner Coroner sounded ahead of their time in 1985. They still do today.
The Swiss thrashers pushed the limits of thrash metal by incorporating jazz, prog-rock, classical and avant-garde elements. This kitchen-sink approach yielded some of the heaviest and most exhilarating albums of the technical thrash scene.
Everything clicked on 1991’s Mental Vortex , which blooms with dark, atmospheric songwriting, jagged riffs and head-spinning solos. Every moment of headbanging brutality is accompanied by a moment of technical grandeur that will leave listeners slack-jawed.
Coroner broke up in 1996 but reunited in 2010. They roared back in 2025 with the mighty Dissonance Theory , their first album in 32 years. SacrifyX, YouTube Forced Entry Years before Soundgarden, Alice in Chains, et al. established Seattle as a grunge hotbed, Forced Entry were storming the Pacific Northwest with their furious and irreverent brand of technical thrash.
Combat Records released their 1989 debut album, Uncertain Future , which won over fans and critics with its mix of speedy brutality, atmospheric guitar work and commanding vocals. But time was not on the band’s side, as 1991’s As Above, So Below arrived with a whimper just months before grunge exploded.
Despite their brain-tickling guitar work, bulldozing grooves and smart-mouth lyrics, a lack of support led to Forced Entry’s dissolution in 1995. Nuclear Blast Records, YouTube Heathen Heathen cut their teeth in the Bay Area thrash scene alongside Testament, Exodus, Death Angel and plenty of other future legends. Although mainstream success eluded the band, they could go toe-to-toe with any of their peers — and maybe even out-muscle and outsmart them.
Heathen proved their mettle on their 1991 sophomore album, Victims of Deception , a collection of shapeshifting tech-thrash opuses. (Imagine if Metallica had kept getting more experimental after … And Justice for All instead of making the Black Album.)
It’s one of the crowning achievements of the subgenre, but it wasn’t enough to keep Heathen together. They disbanded in 1993 but reunited in 2001 and have since released two albums, most recently 2020’s Empire of the Blind . Mekong Delta Anonymity can be a virtue in metal these days. (Just look at Ghost and Sleep Token.) But in the late ‘80s, it might have just obscured the promise of German technical thrash virtuosos Mekong Delta.
Named after a riverbed in Vietnam, Mekong Delta formed in 1985 with the goal to musically outshine their metal peers. They made good on that promise with a series of increasingly technical and wildly ambitious albums, drawing influence from H.P. Lovecraft, classical music and other thrash bands in equal measure.
Mekong Delta reached the pinnacle of their technical thrash powers on 1990’s Dances of Death , which opens with a staggering 20-minute opus. Although they rarely played live and took years to reveal their identities, they remain a rightful cult favorite among fans of big-brained thrash. RockShowTrader, YouTube Toxik Formed in New York in 1985, Toxik signed to Roadrunner Records and issued their debut album, World Circus , in 1987. Teeming with double-bass drum blasts, pummeling riffs and Mike Sanders’ sky-high, quasi-power metal vocals, the album established Toxik as forerunners of the nascent technical thrash metal scene.
Toxik followed up their promising debut with the equally strong and slightly more sophisticated Think This . But after a few more years of heavy touring, they disbanded in 1992.
They’ve since reunited twice and remained active since 2013, releasing two full-lengths, 2018’s Kinetic Closure and 2022’s Dis Morta . Still, they remain a footnote in the thrash metal history books when they deserve at least a few hefty paragraphs of their own. Metaldog38's Home Of Metal, YouTube Watchtower If the technical thrash subgenre has a definitive starting point, it’s Watchtower. The Austin, Texas band ignited a movement with their exhilarating 1985 debut, Energetic Disassembly , featuring Billy White’s angular guitar riffs and Jason McMaster’s skyscraping shrieks.
Following McMaster and White’s departures (with the former going on to Dangerous Toys success), Watchtower recruited vocalist Alan Tecchio and guitarist Ron Jarzombek for their second and final album, 1989’s Control and Resistance. It marked another stone-cold tech-thrash classic, but Tecchio’s exit and Jarzombek’s health issues led to the band’s dissolution in the early ‘90s.
Watchtower might have never achieved mainstream success, but they left a seismic impact on technical thrash and technical death metal, with Death’s Chuck Schuldiner citing them as a major influence. Want more thrash? Check out our list of every thrash metal “Big 4″ album ranked worst to best (we’re still letting the new Megadeth album sink in first, though):
Every Thrash Metal 'Big 4' Album Ranked Every album by Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth and Anthrax get ranked worst to best.
Contributions by Philip Trapp, Ed Rivadavia, Jordan Blum, Ayron Rutan and Joe DiVita. Gallery Credit: Loudwire Staff Tradecraft, Universal 49. Megadeth, 'Super Collider' (2013) “You miss 100 percent of the shots you don’t take,” NHL Hall of Famer Wayne Gretzy once famously said. Unfortunately for Megadeth, they took a huge shot and still missed by a wide margin with 2013’s Super Collider .
It would signal the end for drummer Shawn Drover and guitarist Chris Broderick, not that they had much of a say when it came to the writing anyway. For Mustaine and Ellefson, however, the attempt at a more rock-leaning record is applaudable in theory — they brilliantly pulled this off on Youthanasia and perhaps it was a chance to make good on some other intentions laid out in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s.
Whatever the case, this platter of music is just not good by any measure. It did put Mustaine and co. in position to roar back with a more return-to-roots effort that materialized in 2016’s Dystopia , which is great for the career narrative arc in the long run. There’s a positive! —JD Megaforce Records 48. Anthrax, 'Volume 8: The Threat Is Real' (1998) Not five years removed from 1993’s impressive stylistic reboot for the alt-rock ‘90s that was Sound of White Noise , Anthrax’s career reached a dispiriting nadir with the forgettable – and now virtually forgotten – Volume 8: The Threat is Real . Maybe the band were subconsciously referring to their own dreary career prospects, because they failed to deliver anything else – confidence, decent songs, creative direction – with this miserable set. —ER Capitol 47. Megadeth, 'Risk' (1999) In retrospect, Dave Mustaine should have probably used some of those joint therapy sessions with Lars Ulrich captured for Metallica’s harrowing, inadvertent mockumentary Some Kind of Monster , to explain Megadeth’s own career fiasco, Risk . An ill-advised gambit to push further into the mainstream and even alternative rock, Risk was such a “box office bomb,” that Capitol Records washed their hands of Megadeth after more than a decade. Really, the only thing about this album that makes sense was its title. —ER Elektra 46. Anthrax, 'Stomp 442' (1995) Metal was always part of the Anthrax equation, but the band’s brand of thrash was always cut with something more. In the Joey Belladonna era, that was most noticeably crossover punk and as the band’s style shifted in the ‘90s with John Bush up front, so did the band’s stylistic formula.
Taking cues from the abrasive hardcore of Helmet in particular (at least to these ears), Anthrax moved from the more radio-optimized hard/groove rock of 1993’s Sound of White Noise to what you hear on Stomp 442, which arrived two years later. The first album without guitarist Dan Spitz, Anthrax turned to Pantera legend Dimebag Darrell to play lead on two songs while Paul Crook handled the rest of the studio guitar work opposite Scott Ian.
The intentions were fine, but the execution on the group’s seventh album missed the mark and the lyrics are especially forgettable. The cover art, meanwhile? Memorable for the wrong reasons. —JD Sanctuary Records 45. Megadeth, 'The World Needs A Hero' (2001) Still reeling from the nuclear fallout of 1999’s widely panned Risk , Megadeth entered the new millennium in rebuild mode – in terms of their line-up (Al Pitrelli stepped in for the long-serving Marty Friedman), their music (which thankfully shifted back to metallic norm, if not form), and their reputation (well, good luck with that one). Now signed to Sanctuary, Dave Mustaine and co. tried to overcome persistent issues with songwriting quality with quantity, in what still stands as the longest of all Megadeth albums. —ER Elektra Records 44. Metallica, 'St. Anger' (2003) An extreme sonic direction for the band and the subject of an entire documentary, 2003’s St. Anger has became widely regarded by fans as Metallica’s worst album and has reached a level of memedom in the metal community that few other albums have.
While there are some obvious things to dislike about the record such as drummer Lars Ulrich’s snare sound and the complete absence of Kirk Hammet guitar solos, listeners should not be too quick to dismiss St. Anger. The album is frankly one of Metallica’s most interesting, with introspective lyrical content and variety of both fast and grinding riffs.
Songs such as “Frantic”, “Some Kind of Monster”, and “Invisible Kid” offer a lot to enjoy, but the record’s consistently muddy mix combined with the other shortcomings previously mentioned ultimately leave even more to be desired with this album. —AR Elektra Records 43. Metallica, 'Load' (1996) Released in 1996, Load emerged in a time that wasn’t particularly good to the thrash sub-genre. Alt-rock, grunge, and nu-metal were dominating the charts and Metallica were forced to adapt.
Five years after the release of 1991’s ‘Black Album,’ Load has an even more commercial and hard-rock leaning sound than its predecessor.
It was clear that the band was trying new sounds on tracks such as “Until It Sleeps”, “King Nothing”, and “The Outlaw Torn”, which, fast forward today, are widely loved by fans. While it’s sonic direction has unfortunately landed it at the bottom of many fans’ favorite Metallica album lists, Load is a perfectly enjoyable hard rock album by a band who at the time was just looking to try something different. —AR Megaforce Records 42. Anthrax, 'State of Euphoria' (1988) Over 30 years later, it’s hard to understand the exaggerated amount of negative feedback that was heaped upon Anthrax’s fourth studio album, 1988’s State of Euphoria . So, it was Among the Living , Part 2 … so what? Do you know how many bands would give their eye-teeth to conjure up anything worthy of that ‘put down’? Pretty much any band outside of thrash’s Big Four, that’s who, including Anthrax themselves, post 1991. —ER Sanctuary, Nuclear Blast 41. Anthrax, 'We've Come For You All' (2003) After the triple whammy of the career low that was 1998’s Volume 8: The Threat is Real , the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, and the mysterious letters laced with deadly anthrax – the poisonous substance, not the band – Anthrax briefly considered changing their name! But the New Yorkers duly rebounded with a much-improved fourth and final album behind frontman John Bush, We’ve Come for You All . It didn’t solve Anthrax’s diminished popularity issues, but it paved the way to a reunion with Joey Belladonna and stronger albums to come. —ER American Recordings 40. Slayer, 'Diabolus In Musica' (1998) Simultaneously Slayer’s most experimental and concession-filled album (if that’s even possible), 1998’s Diabolus in Musica arrived during one of the most fallow and hostile periods in heavy metal history, when the style had yet to free itself of the alt-rock-imposed purgatory. But Slayer didn’t help their cause (nor did their fan-base, one of the most resistant-to-change in metal) by consorting with nu-metal, dropped tunings, and other gimmicks that simply didn’t serve the band’s ascetic tradition. Simply put, this was a dead end. —ER Roadrunner 39. Megadeth, 'Th1rt3en' (2011) Megadeth’s thirteenth studio album sadly fulfilled the prophecy of its title, in spite of bassist Dave Ellefson’s return following a decade in exile, and maintained the negative trajectory of its predecessor, Endgame , by notching fewer sales, fewer quality tracks (a standout here, “Black Swan” had been an outtake from the formidable United Abominations ), and fewer fans who could be bothered. Heck, even Vic Rattlehead refused to show his face on this competent, not exactly lousy, but ultimately workmanlike Megadeth LP. —ER Elektra Records 38. Metallica, 'Reload' (1997) If Metallica had only come clean and called 1997’s Reload what it was: an album made up of all the songs that weren’t deemed good or gutsy enough for the previous year’s risk-taking Load , plus a few newbies for good measure, critical and consumer response may have been a little more positive. But for younger fans checking into the Reload hotel without all that baggage, its many bland – or worse – downright irritating songs (e.g. “The Memory Remains,” “The Unforgiven II”) will likely seem like a decent, if unexciting collection, somewhat akin to a third-rate repetition of ‘The Black Album.’ —ER Nuclear Blast 37. Slayer, 'Repentless' (2015) Just as some fans never came to terms with hearing anyone but Dave Lombardo behind Slayer’s drum kit, there are those who could never stomach the thought of anyone filling Jeff Hanneman’s boots after his untimely death in 2013. But few would dispute the fact that no one was more qualified for this unenviable task than Exodus leader Gary Holt, who brought his unquestionable instrumental credentials to bear on 2015’s potent Repentless , and managed to do both himself and Hannenman’s memory proud. —ER Warner Bros. Records 36. Metallica, 'Death Magnetic' (2008) The Rick Rubin-produced Death Magnetic is a safe but fervent return to form, as well as the band’s best LP since 1991’s Metallica . Punctuated by awesome guitar solos and stellar bass playing from newcomer Robert Trujillo, there’s a ton to like. Specifically, “That Was Just Your Life” and “The Judas Kiss” strike a satisfying balance between familiarity and freshness, just as “Suicide & Redemption” effectively calls back to some earlier instrumentals. “The Unforgiven III” continues the saga with enticing heart and hecticness, too, and “All Nightmare Long” is overwhelmingly feisty.
Honestly, the whole thing is a transparent yet thrilling emulation of Metallica’s former glory, which is really all it needed to be at the time. —JB American Recordings, Sony Music 35. Slayer, 'World Painted Blood' (2009) World Painted Blood was Slayer’s tenth studio LP (eleventh if you count the punk covers set, Undisputed Attitude ) and second to feature the reunited Araya/Hanneman/King/Lombardo quartet … so, what could possibly go wrong? Well, quite a bit, actually, because while they checked all the right boxes, even the most satisfying thrashers here felt a little too self-aware about walking the sonic tightrope of fan expectations. Call it Slayer-by-numbers, if you will: just what the doctor ordered for many loyalists, but a sign of trouble (and Hanneman’s declining health) in the years ahead. —ER Sanctuary Records 34. Megadeth, 'The System Has Failed' (2004) It’s basically a Mustaine solo album fleshed out by session musicians and guests (including ex-guitarist Chris Poland). Considering its hodgepodge line-up, alongside the fact that it arrived shortly after Mustaine’s radial neuropathy scare, it’s a miracle that it turned out so much better than its immediate predecessors. In particular, “The Scorpion” is enormously confident and catchy, “I Know Jack” features sublime dual guitarwork and both “Of Mice and Men” and “Die Dead Enough” are surprisingly mellow and endearing. A couple of clunkers aside (“Blackmail the Universe” and “Kick the Chair”), The System Has Failed is a rousing and promising comeback. —JB Capitol Records 33. Megadeth, 'So Far, So Good... So what?' (1988) The first album following the firing of drummer Gar Samuelson and guitarist Chris Poland, So Far, So Good… So What! proved the band could stay consistent with their sound regardless of personnel. The record kicks off with “Into The Lungs of Hell”, a triumphant instrumental track that includes layers of horn, flute, and percussion samples at its beginning before hard transitioning into the shredding guitars and blistering drums we all know Megadeth so well for. Other incredibly fast and heavy tracks such as “Set The World Afire” and “In My Darkest Hour” make So Far, So Good… So What! a memorable record in Megadeth’s discography, and one that may fly under the radar compared to its successor in Rust In Peace, even if it does have some tracks that haven’t stood the test of time quite as those choice cuts. —AR American Recordings 32. Slayer, 'Divine Intervention' (1994) Divine Intervention , a.k.a. Dave Lombardo’s ‘told-you-so’ album, proved that not even a superior technician like Paul Bostaph could swing at breakneck speeds, while confirming that the Slayer aesthetic was indeed an almost perfect and immutable monolith, not to be tinkered with. All that being said, although Araya, Hanneman and King’s doomed attempt to revive the hallowed, white-knuckle intensity of Reign in Blood was something they simply had to try, if only to stop fans and critics continually asking them to. —ER Roadrunner 31. Megadeth, 'United Abominations' (2007) United Abominations needed to confirm that The System Has Failed wasn’t a fluke, that Megadeth’s move to Roadrunner Records was a good decision and that their new line-up was up to snuff. Fortunately, it did all of that and more. Aside from showcasing some of their coolest riffs in ages on “Washington Is Next!” the album radiates robust cohesion and chemistry. This is most apparent on the efficiently theatrical “Sleepwalker” and the slightly psychedelic “Never Walk Alone... A Call to Arms.” However divisive, the remake of “A Tout Le Monde” (with Lacuna Coil’s Cristina Scabbia) is a great touch, too. —JB Megaforce Records 30. Anthrax, 'Fistful of Metal' (1984) All glory to the departed Jonny Z of Megaforce Records for signing a persistent Anthrax and ushering unto the world their NWOBHM-inflected debut, 1984’s Fistful of Metal . It’s their only album with singer Neil Turbin and is one of the most underrated albums amid the breadth of the Big 4 catalog.
While many of these cuts aren’t well-remembered by any stretch beyond the opening salvo of “Deathrider” and “Metal Thrashing Mad,” there’s really nothing wrong or even bad about any of the songs here. It just lacks the songwriting maturity and a more defined style Anthrax would quickly find after this release, but for any insatiable classic metal enthusiast, Fistful more than scratches that nagging itch and the playing feels well beyond their years. —JD Blackened Recordings 29. Metallica, 'Hardwired to Self-Destruct' (2016) If Death Magnetic proved that Metallica could still do it, successor Hardwired... to Self-Destruct proved that they wanted to still do it. With better songwriting, musicianship and production than its predecessor, it’s a spirited statement of purpose from start to finish. Starter “Hardwired” recalls the musical and lyrical revolt of their first few outings, and that awe-inspiring abrasiveness carries through to “Moth into Flame” and “Halo on Fire” (among other highlights). Sure, the second half isn’t quite as strong – “ManUNkind” and “Murder One” are at least a bit bland – yet closer “Spit Out the Bone” kicks plenty of ass. —JB American Recordings 28. Slayer, 'God Hates Us All' (2001) Infamously released on Sept. 11, 2001, God Hates Us All marked the end of Slayer’s misguided and half-hearted attempts at self-parody ( Divine Intervention ) and reinvention ( Diabolus in Musica ) with a production that was intentionally redolent of the band’s classic sound. Yes, they still took a few missteps (see the nu-metal-influenced “Threshold” and WWE commission “Here Comes the Pain”), but the semi-title track “Disciple” and other modern classics set the stage for the fantastic Christ Illusion five years later. —ER Universal 27. Megadeth, 'Dystopia' (2016) Wow, talk about a rebound! After the dreary Th1rt3en and (especially) Super Collider , few Megadeth listeners had high hopes for Dystopia . But, fresh talent often yields fresh techniques, so bringing in drummer Chris Adler and guitarist Kiko Loureiro definitely energized their formula. “The Threat is Real'' is a characteristically invigorating wakeup call musically and thematically, whereas “Fatal Illusion” is irresistibly blunt and barbaric and “Poisonous Shadows” is deceptively multifaceted. The acoustic and electric balance within “Conquer or Die!” is superb, too, and throughout the journey, Mustaine’s gruff singing matches his condemnatory songwriting. Even the album cover is a sizable improvement. —JB Roadrunner 26. Megadeth, 'Endgame' (2009) Poised to be the pinnacle of Megadeth’s 2000s rejuvenation, Endgame is more polarizing than its two precursors (at least in hindsight). That said, it undoubtedly excels in several spots. Instrumental opener “Dialectic Chaos” mixes their thrash foundation with shades of Swedish melodeath masters such as In Flames and At the Gates. It’s a thunderously complex beginning that slyly bleeds into the feverishly assured “This Day We Fight!”
Near the end, “How the Story Ends” merges hooky vocals with virtuosic guitarwork and percussion before “The Right to Go Insane” marries relatable lyricism with alluringly rebellious arrangements. Standouts such as “Bite the Hand” and “Head Crusher” appear in-between, and bolstered by Andy Sneap’s typically outstanding production, Endgame is generally a commendable way to wrap up the decade. —JB American Recordings 25. Slayer, 'Christ Illusion' (2006) Chances are that a primed and salivating Slayer fan base would have embraced pretty much any kind of album from the “classic,” reunited Araya/Hanneman/King/Lombardo line-up. But Christ Illusion , the fearsome foursome’s first foray into the studio together in 16 years actually delivered on its promise. Yes, this time, everything came together: the music, the performances, the attitude, and even the blasphemous cover designed by Reign in Blood artist Larry Carroll (the only person missing was producer Rick Rubin, but he wasn’t missed), making this the first Slayer album most everyone could get behind since Seasons in the Abyss . —ER Combat Records 24. Megadeth, 'Killing Is My Business... And Business Is Good!' (1985) In his 2010 memoir, Dave Mustaine remarks: “After getting fired from Metallica, all I remember is that I wanted blood. Theirs. I wanted to be faster and heavier than them.” To his credit, that spiteful ambition permeates every inch of Megadeth’s debut record. Primarily, he included “Mechanix” (a punkier variant of Metallica’s “The Four Horsemen”) to “straighten [them] up.” That ceaseless belligerence spearheads most of the remaining tracks (especially the title track, “Rattlehead” and “Chosen Ones”), underscoring Mustaine’s arguably superior skills, while “These Boots” and “Last Rites/Loved to Death” display his willingness to venture beyond genre conventions from the jump. —JB Elektra 23. Anthrax, 'Sound of White Noise' (1993) The ‘90s was a time of change for thrash artists who rose to prominence just a few years earlier. Almost everyone veered off in wildly different directions (or just simply disbanded) and after the thought-provoking Persistence of Time, Anthrax replaced singer Joey Belladonna with Armored Saint’s John Bush and dialed back the complexity of the music.
With grunge and alternative influences now firmly in their grasp, Anthrax navigated an unexpected turn remarkably well on Sound of White Noise, which peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard 200 (the band’s highest chart spot ever) and was certified Gold within two months of release.
Whether it was the outright intent to adopt a more radio-friendly and commercially relevant sound or it just happened that way doesn’t really matter all these decades later. This is a dynamic, exciting record with a timeless production that is easily one of metal’s most underrated releases. —JD Megaforce Records, Nuclear Blast 22. Anthrax, 'Worship Music' (2011) The reinstatement of classic era vocalist Joey Belladonna served to restore Anthrax’s mojo and an eight year absence from the studio helped to replenish their songwriting cupboard, leading to a potent return to form on 2011’s cleverly titled Worship Music . No, its songs were never going to scale the same heights as those vintage ‘80s releases, but they satisfied most fans’ high expectations, and certainly their nostalgia for the classic Anthrax line-up, finally reunited after some 20 years. —ER Blackened Recordings 21. Metallica, '72 Seasons' (2023) At 77 minutes, 72 Seasons is a lot to digest, but even so, it's the one 21st century album most fans seem to be on the same page about, celebrating its greatness quite a lot more than panning the minimal lowlights.
James Hetfield is the star here with one of the most powerful vocal performances of his recording career and its the cherry-topper that makes the music even more convincing.
Metallica haven't sounded this youthful since, arguably, The Black Album. —JD Universal Music Group 20. Megadeth, 'The Sick, The Dying... And the Dead!' Six long, long years after the release of Dystopia (which earned Megadeth their first-ever Grammy for the title track), Dave Mustaine and crew return with The Sick, The Dying… And The Dead!. Too much has happened between records to recap here, but it’s been a hard-fought and well-won battle getting to this stage and, damn, did these vets deliver on a record that speaks to the breadth of the Megadeth catalog. “We’ll Be Back,” the lead single, is a face-melter in the purest sense and a great first impression of drummer Dirk Verbeuren, who makes his first studio appearance with them after joining in 2016. It’s all the reassurance anyone needed about what this album had in store. Elsewhere, there’s more pummeling doses of speed and adrenaline (“Night Stalkers”), as well as old school, traditional metal (“Célebutante”), mid-tempo corkers (“Soldier On!”), a daring, frenzied thrash ballad (“Dogs of Chernobyl”), and cinematic sci-fi (“Mission to Mars), making it one of the most well-rounded Megadeth records ever. —JD Capitol Records 19. Megadeth, 'Cryptic Writings' (1997) What Cryptic Writings lacks in top-to-bottom strength, it more than makes up for with a handful of high quality songs — “Trust,” “She-Wolf,” “Almost Honest” and “A Secret Place,” many of which remain setlist staples more than 25 years later.
This album, the last with drummer Nick Menza, treads a similar path walked by its predecessor, only with a more open songwriting palette. It’s a bit uneven though as Megadeth wade through post-grunge filtered by ‘70s rock (“I’ll Get Even”), their thrashing heyday (“The Disintegrators”), stubborn-rhythm hard rock (“Sin”) and more. —JD Megaforce Records, Nuclear Blast 18. Anthrax, 'For All Kings' (2017) The first from Anthrax to feature guitarist Jon Donais (Shadows Fall), For All Kings is a devastatingly effective merging of the band’s classic late ‘80s style thrash and completely modern elements, some of which border on hard rock. Knowing the band’s affinity for acts such as Kansas and Journey, it’s easy to see where this songwriting dynamic came from, but “Breathing Lightning” and “Monster at the End” in particular lean far into the rock direction, doesn’t come off as dated one bit.
With an album that clocks in at just under one hour, diversity from front to back is so crucial. “Evil Twins” is a dark thrasher, “Blood Eagle Wings” is ridiculously epic and “All Of Them Thieves” brings the groove that dominated the Anthrax ‘90s sound. A true late-career gem here. —JD Capitol Records 17. Megadeth, 'Youthanasia' (1994) "Welcome Back to Megadeth, Arizona." Some fans might not remember the digital postcard that greeted visitors to the first official website for a band, launched by Capitol Records in 1994 for Megadeth's sixth album, Youthanasia . But fans of all ages can still return to the album itself, which found Dave Mustaine and co. sharpening the streamlined brand of heavy metal they developed after their thrash years. (Two sumptuous singles also played a part, "Train of Consequences" and "A Tout le Monde.") And, in all actuality, you can still revisit the old website, too — just type www.hollywoodandvine.com/megadeth into the Wayback Machine. —PT Metal Blade Records 16. Slayer, 'Show No Mercy' (1983) An album unlike any other in the Slayer catalog, Show No Mercy is oh so typical of countless bands’ first albums where you can hear more of their influences than you can hear the direction they’d eventually take. And that’s what makes debuts so enthralling — where else are you going to hear this band fully embrace classic metal triumph as they grappled with the anthemic moments of Judas Priest and the mangled, snarling, Satanic punk-metal of Venom?
The 1983 record has held up remarkably well and still sounds menacingly evil with far more tracks that are still championed by fans today than there ones that have been resigned to somewhat obscurity. —JD Elektra Records 15. Metallica, 'Metallica' (1991) The album that introduced Metallica to the mainstream is still their most accessible effort. It's also nearly a "greatest hits" in and of itself, considering it contains five RIAA platinum or gold-certified singles. That's the most on any Metallica album before or since. And all five numbers — "Enter Sandman," "The Unforgiven," "Nothing Else Matters, "Wherever I May Roam" and "Sad But True" — remain instantly recognizable. No wonder this effort got the remaster and reissue treatment for its 30th anniversary in 2021. Not to mention an expansive cover songs album with over 50 other artists paying tribute to it. —PT Metal Blade Records 14. Slayer, 'Hell Awaits' (1985) This is where they went from Slayer to FUCKING SL YEERRRR! A couple more A’s and R’s would get added to that primal roar a couple years later with Reign In Blood, but we’re getting ahead of ourselves…
Revisionist history, for better or for worse, affords us the ability to claim wild things such as, “You can just tell they were about to do something huge,” but the progression from Show No Mercy to Hell Awaits not only shows identity taking shape, but that Slayer were rather distant from the their thrash peers in California. This is a seriously sinister album that’s heavier on atmosphere than any other thrash record at the time. —JD Megaforce Records 13. Anthrax, 'Spreading the Disease' (1985) The introductions of bassist Frank Bello and vocalist Joey Belladonna are but two of the many reasons for why Spreading the Disease bested its predecessor by a country mile. After all, the former brought plenty of dexterity to the rhythm section while the latter’s technically superior singing – when judged against Neil Turbin – allowed for more variety and charisma. Of course, the returning trio upped their game as well, resulting in captivating belters such as “Aftershock,” “Gung-Ho” and “Medusa.”
Elsewhere, “Madhouse” and “S.S.C./Stand or Fall” highlight the group’s accessibility and tunefulness (compared to the other three major thrash titans, anyway).
Rather than succumb to the dreaded “sophomore slump,” then, Spreading the Disease jump started Anthrax’s classic period. —JB Megaforce Records 12. Anthrax, 'Persistence of Time' (1990) It might be Anthrax’s most creatively grave and clever work – for artistic and interpersonal reasons – and it’s a clear response to the relative safety and frivolity of State of Euphoria . The words and music of “Blood” and “Discharge” reveal a palpable darkness and depth, imploring everyone to hear them with utmost seriousness. Similarly, instrumental “Intro to Reality” is strikingly vivid, challenging and affective, and their take on Joe Jackson’s “Got the Time” is effectively idiosyncratic yet faithful. The fact that it’s Joey Belladonna’s last full-length record with Anthrax for over 20 years (until 2011’s Worship Music ) adds to its distinction. —JB Capitol Records 11. Megadeth, 'Countdown to Extinction' (1992) When Megadeth entered the studio in the fall of 1991, they had a choice to make — they could write and record another album full of complex rhythms and virtuosic solos, or they could go in a different direction.
On Countdown To Extinction , the band chose the latter.
The record features a more commercially driven sound then previous projects, but not to the discredit of the music. After all, it features some of the band’s most loved and recognizable songs in “Symphony of Destruction”, “Sweating Bullets”, and “Skin O’ My Teeth”. At its core, Countdown To Extinction is an extremely straightforward and politically charged thrash record that could go toe to toe with many other albums on this list. —AR Elektra Records 10. Metallica, '...And Justice For All' (1988) Following the sudden death of bassist Cliff Burton and landmark success of Master of Puppets , the Grammy-nominated ...And Justice for All showcased Metallica’s steadfast resilience. True, you can barely hear newcomer Jason Newsted’s contributions, but what is audible is proof enough that he belongs. Plus, the record saw the quartet leaning further into adventurous progressive metal territory, especially with the blockbuster title track, “To Live is To Die” and “Harvester of Sorrow.” There’s also the beautiful “One,” which led to the band’s first music video, and in general, the LP found them at their most daring and developed stage. —JB Megaforce Records 9. Metallica, 'Kill 'Em All' (1983) Ah, that one that started it all. Originally known as Metal Up Your Ass and released on Jon Zazula’s Megaforce Records, it’s a seminal thrash/speed metal collection that remains one of Metallica’s finest hours. Opener “Hit the Lights” immediately captures the group’s dynamic instrumental interplay and characteristically gruff vocals. It’s simultaneously bestial and complex, as are “Motorbreath” and fan favorites “Whiplash” and “Seek & Destroy.” Meanwhile, Dave Mustaine’s co-written “The Four Horsemen” brilliantly introduces the multifaceted song structures both Metallica and Megadeth would later perfect. It’s undeniably rough around the edges, but that’s part of what makes it a classic. —JB Def Jam Recordings 8. Slayer, 'South of Heaven' (1988) Considering that guitarist Kerry King and drummer Dave Lombardo have been critical of South of Heaven in later years, you might expect it to be lackluster. However, the intentionally slower and cleaner follow-up to Reign in Blood is an absolute beast. The title track – alongside “Read Between the Lies” and “Live Undead” – trudges more than terrorizes, but there’s easily enough grittiness to appeal. Plus, the acoustic start of “Spill the Blood” is a welcomed change of pace, whereas “Cleanse the Soul” and “Silent Scream” rarely skimp on hyperactive sinisterness.
Echoing Show No Mercy , Hell Awaits and Reign in Blood in different ways, South of Heaven is a superb amalgamation of the band’s aesthetic thus far. —JB Capitol Records 7. Megadeth, 'Peace Sells... But Who's Buying?' (1986) The album where Megadeth came into their own. The Dave Mustaine-led band's second studio effort, 1986's Peace Sells… But Who's Buying? established the act as a force-to-be-reckoned-with in the otherwise long shadow of Metallica, the group from which Mustaine originally hailed. And after Megadeth released a sufficiently hearty debut album the year prior, Mustaine's songcraft came to the fore on Peace Sells' explosively arranged songs such as "The Conjuring" and the truncated title track. Even something as seemingly inconsequential as the latter tune's bass guitar intro — performed on record by bassist David Ellefson but composed by Mustaine — was enshrined in music fans' memories as the opening tag on MTV News . —PT Def American Records 6. Slayer, 'Seasons In The Abyss' (1990) Seasons in the Abyss marked the end of the first Lombardo era and the final entry into cover artist Larry Carroll’s initial trilogy. (Coincidentally, both would return for 2006’s Christ Illusion .) That alone would be worth celebrating, but luckily, it’s packed with colossal tunes as well. In fact, it essentially fuses the melodic reprieves of South of Heaven with the crushing speed of Reign in Blood , as evidenced on standouts such as “War Ensemble,” “Temptation” and “Born of Fire.” Additionally, “Seasons in the Abyss” is an epic and emotional career staple. Like Metallica’s Death Magnetic , the set doubles down on prior strengths rather than innovates, but it’s difficult to complain when it’s done this well. —JB Megaforce Records 5. Metallica, 'Ride The Lightning' (1984) Metal fans could tell Metallica were feeling the thunder when the band released their second album, Ride the Lightning , in 1984. A sonic improvement over their debut from the previous year, it introduced some of Metallica's now-classic anthems, such as "For Whom the Bell Tolls'' and "Fade to Black." Both songs proved the lightning-quick metalheads could get some groove going when they wanted to. After all, this album represents the most substantial creative leap Metallica had yet taken. And they wouldn't stop taking them. —PT Megaforce Records 4. Anthrax, 'Among The Living' (1987) Famously, Anthrax enlisted legendary producer/engineer Eddie Kramer to capture their live vitality. It’s clear within the first few moments of the monumental title track that he totally nailed it, leading to an album ripe with mosh-worthy agility and hostility. Just listen to the pulsating percussion of “Efilnikufesin (N.F.L.)” or the anthemic cheers of “One World” for proof. Seeing as how metal often connects to geek culture, the LP’s allusions to Stephen King (“A Skeleton in the Closet” and “Among the Living”) and comic book badass Judge Dredd (“I Am the Law”) cemented Anthrax’s drive to deliver exactly what audiences craved (and what the genre needed). —JB Capitol Records 3. Megadeth, 'Rust In Peace' (1990) Rust in Peace is one of the most refined thrash metal albums of the initial era. Perhaps it's because Megadeth finally got clean from drugs on this one. Either way, while closing the door on their '80s iterations, on this recording, Megadeth found their classic band lineup. It's their first with virtuoso guitarist Marty Friedman and the late drummer Nick Menza, and both players' presence makes the record what it is. Sure, bandleader Dave Mustaine likely (and bizarrely) re-recorded all the vocals in 2004 — or undoubtedly much more than he said he did — but it doesn't detract from the album's oomph. Wage the war. —PT Def Jam Recordings 2. Slayer 'Reign In Blood' (1986) As with Metallica and Master of Puppets , it’s Slayer’s third LP – Reign in Blood – that remains their signature sequence and one of the top three trash metal albums of all time. From its beautifully macabre cover to its honed chemistry of focused and ferocious hookiness, it’s masterful. Of course, “Raining Blood” makes for an iconic finale – its seamless emergence from the militaristic “Postmortem” is downright ingenious – but everything that comes before it is nearly faultless, too. For instance, “Angel of Death” is delightfully visceral in multiple ways, “Jesus Saves” is an increasingly relevant rebuttal of oppressive dogma and both “Epidemic” and “Necrophobic” are relentlessly agitated.
In less than 30 minutes, Slayer cemented their genre supremacy. —JB Elektra Records 1. Metallica, 'Master of Puppets' (1986) We wouldn't even have metalcore — or who knows how many variations of brutal guitar chug — without this, Metallica's watershed 1986 studio collection. Very likely the best and most defining document of thrash metal overall, it is undoubtedly the greatest release among all the full-length efforts from the big four thrash acts. And as the last testament to the arrangement skills of the late Metallica bassist Cliff Burton, even the "gotcha" acoustic opening is as effective as it was over 35 years ago. You can still feel the pure metal power when the distortion kicks in. Master of Puppets stands alone. —PT Subscribe to Loudwire on YouTube .
summary: But for younger fans checking into the Reload hotel without all that baggage, its many bland – or worse – downright irritating songs (e.g. “The Memory Remains,” “The Unforgiven II”) will likely seem like a decent, if unexciting collection, somewhat akin to a third-rate repetition of ‘The Black Album.’ —ER Nuclear Blast 37. Elsewhere, there’s more pummeling doses of speed and adrenaline (“Night Stalkers”), as well as old school, traditional metal (“Célebutante”), mid-tempo corkers (“Soldier On!”), a daring, frenzied thrash ballad (“Dogs of Chernobyl”), and cinematic sci-fi (“Mission to Mars), making it one of the most well-rounded Megadeth records ever.
